title: Subordinate Clauses
summary: Beyond the *kad* and *ar* of ¶109–¶110: time with *kai* and *kol*, concession with *nors*, and the Lithuanian habit of keeping the tense that was meant rather than shifting it as English does.

rules.heading: Kai: When
rules.statement: **Kai** introduces a **time** clause — *when*, *as*. It was listed among the vocabulary of the future (¶103); it is now needed as a full subordinator. The clause it opens is set off by a comma, as every subordinate clause is (¶109), and the tense inside it is the tense of the event itself: present for present, past for past, future for future.

examples.gloss: When it rains, I read at home.

examples.target: Kai jis atėjo, mes jau valgėme.
examples.gloss: When he came, we were already eating.
Ring me when you get back.
examples.note: future in the *kai*-clause, as the return is future

footnotes: *Kada* asks *when?*; *kai* answers it in a statement. The two are not interchangeable: *Kada grįši?* but *Paskambink, kai grįši.*

rules.heading: Kol: While and Until
rules.statement: **Kol** covers the ground of English *while* and *until*, according to the sense of the verbs. With two actions that overlap it is *while*; with one that stops at the start of another it is *until*. A negative in the *kol*-clause often marks the *until* reading: *laukiau, kol jis atėjo* against *dirbau, kol jis neatėjo* — I waited until he came / I worked until he came (literally *while he had not come*).

rows.label: limit + ne-
cells: I shall work until I finish.

examples.gloss: I waited until the bus arrived.
While it is raining, we shall stay at home.

rules.heading: Nors: Although
rules.statement: **Nors** (and the fuller **nors ir**) introduces a **concession** — *although*, *even though*. The main clause often answers with **vis tiek** (*all the same*) or simply continues; nothing in the grammar of *nors* requires a special mood. English *although* with a past in the subordinate clause does not force a tense shift in Lithuanian either.

examples.target: Nors buvo šalta, ėjome į parką.
examples.gloss: Although it was cold, we went to the park.

examples.target: Nors jis dirba daug, vis tiek nespėja.
examples.gloss: Although he works a lot, he still does not manage in time.
I shall come even though it is raining.

footnotes: *Bet* contradicts; *nors* concedes. *Norėjau eiti, bet nebuvo laiko* cancels the wish; *Nors nebuvo laiko, ėjau* admits the obstacle and goes anyway.

rules.heading: The Comma before Every Subordinate Clause
rules.statement: Lithuanian punctuates by **grammar**, not by pause. Wherever a clause introduced by *kad, ar, kai, kol, nors, jeigu, nes* begins, a **comma** stands before it — even when English would write none. The rule of ¶109 for *kad* is therefore the rule for the whole system: learn the comma with the conjunction.

examples.gloss: I shall come although it will be late.

rules.heading: Sequence of Tenses
rules.statement: Lithuanian does **not** shift tenses in reported or subordinate clauses the way English does. What was said in the future stays in the future; what was present stays present. *Jis sakė, kad ateis* is *he said he would come*, but Lithuanian keeps *ateis*. The same honesty of tense holds after *kai, kol, nors* and *jeigu*: choose the tense that names the time of the event, not a tense forced by the main verb.

paradigms.caption: English shifts; Lithuanian keeps

rows.label: kai + past
cells: When I came, he was reading.

rows.label: jeigu + future
cells: If you have time, we shall go.

paradigms.footnote: The English present after *if* and the English back-shift after *said* are both interference to unlearn. Lithuanian says what it means.

examples.gloss: She thought that I was ill.
examples.note: present *sergu* kept under a past main verb

examples.gloss: When I return, I shall tell you.

rules.heading: The Inventory so Far
rules.statement: The subordinators now in hand fall into clear jobs. **Kad** reports a statement; **ar** reports a yes-or-no question; **kai** and **kol** fix time; **nors** concedes; **jeigu** conditions; **nes** gives a reason that cannot open the sentence. Coordinators (*ir, bet, o, arba*) join equals and take no comma of subordination. Mixing the jobs — *jeigu* for *ar*, *kai* for *kada* in a question — is the usual error at this level.

examples.target: Nežinau, ar jis ateis, kai lyja.
examples.gloss: I do not know whether he will come when it rains.

examples.target: Nors jis sakė, kad ateis, aš lauksiu, kol paskambins.
examples.gloss: Although he said he would come, I shall wait until he rings.

vocabulary.notes: Time subordinator; comma before the clause.
Also nors ir; often answered by vis tiek.

vocabulary.gloss: not to manage in time, to fail to catch
vocabulary.notes: Negation of spėti; cited as learners meet the form.

drills.stem: Complete: **____ lyja, aš skaitau namie.** (When it rains…)
drills.explanation: **Kai** introduces a time clause in a statement. *Kada* asks the question *when?*; *kad* reports a statement; *ar* reports a yes-or-no question.

drills.stem: Complete: **Palauk, ____ ateisiu.** (Wait until I come.)
drills.explanation: **Kol** is *until* when one action waits for the start of another. *Kai* would be a plain *when*, and *nors* a concession.

drills.stem: Which conjunction means **although**?
drills.explanation: **Nors** concedes. *nes* gives a reason, *todėl* a consequence, *kol* a time limit.

drills.stem: Complete: **Nors buvo šalta, ____ į parką.**
drills.explanation: The concession is past (*buvo šalta*), and the main action is past with it: **ėjome**. Tense follows the time of the event (¶183).

drills.stem: Which sentences are correctly punctuated?
drills.explanation: A comma stands before every subordinate clause. The second and fourth omit it before *kol* and before the main clause after a fronted *kai*-clause — both need the comma: *Palauk, kol…* and *Kai lyja, aš…*.

drills.stem: **Jis sakė, kad ateis.** Why not a past in the second clause?
options: Because Lithuanian keeps the tense that was meant; he said *I shall come*.
Because *sakė* forbids any past after it.
drills.explanation: Sequence of tenses in Lithuanian is honest reporting: the future *ateis* stays. English back-shifts to *would come*; Lithuanian does not.

drills.stem: Complete: **Paskambink man, kai ____.** (Ring me when you get back.)
drills.explanation: The return is future, so the *kai*-clause takes the future **grįši**. The infinitive and the conditional are the wrong mood and tense.

drills.stem: Which uses of **kol** are correct?
drills.explanation: *Kol* is a subordinator, not a question word — *when?* is *kada?*. The first is *while*, the second and fourth *until*.

drills.stem: Which conjunction fits: **____ jis dirba daug, vis tiek nespėja.**
drills.explanation: The main clause concedes an obstacle and continues anyway — that is **nors**, answered here by *vis tiek*. *Nes* would give a reason for the main clause, which is the wrong relation.

drills.stem: Which of these are **subordinators**?
drills.explanation: *kai*, *nors*, and *jeigu* open subordinate clauses. *ir* is a coordinator.

drills.stem: **Kai atėjau, jis skaitė.** What does the tense pair show?
options: That each clause keeps the tense of its own event: both past.
That the main clause must be present after *kai*.
drills.explanation: Both events are past, so both verbs are past. There is no special sequence rule beyond naming each event's time.

drills.title: Lietus ir darbas
drills.passage:
Rūta sakė, kad rytoj dirbs namie, kai lyja. Kol lietus nustos, ji nesiruošia eiti į miestą. Nors draugė kvietė į kavinę, Rūta atsakė:
RŪTA. Ačiū, bet aš palauksiu, kol baigsiu darbą. Jeigu oras bus geresnis, paskambinsiu.
Draugė nežinojo, ar Rūta tikrai ateis, nes Rūta dažnai keičia planus.
DRAUGĖ. Gerai. Lauksiu, nors ir vėluosiu į teatrą.
drills.translation: Rūta said that tomorrow she would work at home when it rains. Until the rain stops, she does not mean to go into town. Although a friend invited her to a café, Rūta answered: "Thanks, but I shall wait until I finish the work. If the weather is better, I shall ring." The friend did not know whether Rūta would really come, because Rūta often changes plans. "All right," she said. "I shall wait, even though I shall be late for the theatre."

questions.explanation: *Rūta sakė, kad rytoj dirbs namie, kai lyja.* The café is what the friend invited her to, and she put it off.

questions.stem: Kodėl draugė nežinojo, ar Rūta ateis?
questions.explanation: *nes Rūta dažnai keičia planus.* *Nes* introduces the reason directly.

questions.stem: What did Rūta say she would do tomorrow if it rains?
questions.explanation: *sakė, kad rytoj dirbs namie, kai lyja* — reported statement with *kad*, time clause with *kai*, future kept under a past main verb.

questions.stem: Which subordinators appear in the passage?
questions.explanation: *kad*, *kol* (twice), *nors* (twice), and also *jeigu*, *ar*, *nes* — but *arba* is a coordinator and does not appear.

questions.stem: **Draugė nežinojo, ar Rūta tikrai ateis** — why *ar*?
options: Because a yes-or-no question is being reported.
Because the clause is a concession.
questions.explanation: Indirect yes-or-no questions take **ar** (¶110). *Jeigu* would make a condition; *nors* a concession; *nes* a reason.

questions.stem: **Lauksiu, nors ir vėluosiu į teatrą.** What is the relation between the clauses?
options: Cause: she waits because she will be late.
Concession: she will wait even though it makes her late.
Time: she waits until she is late.
questions.explanation: **Nors ir** concedes the drawback. The futures in both clauses name future events without English-style shifting.

questions.stem: How many times does **kol** appear in the passage?
questions.explanation: Twice: *Kol lietus nustos…* and *palauksiu, kol baigsiu darbą* — both in the *until* reading.

sources.citation: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.), *Lithuanian Grammar*. Vilnius: Baltos lankos, 1997.

drills.stem: Complete: **Paskambink man, ____ grįši.** (Ring me when you get back.)
drills.explanation: **Kai** in a statement; *kada* asks the question *when?*

drills.stem: Complete: **____ buvo šalta, ėjome į parką.** (Although it was cold…)
drills.explanation: **Nors** concedes. *Bet* would cancel rather than concede.

drills.stem: Complete: **Laukiau, ____ autobusas atvažiavo.** (I waited until the bus arrived.)
drills.explanation: **Kol** for *until* when one action stops at another's start.

drills.stem: Which is correctly punctuated?
drills.explanation: A comma stands **before** every subordinate clause: *Žinau, kad…*

drills.stem: **Jis sakė, kad ateis.** Why *ateis*, not an English-style past?
options: Lithuanian keeps the tense of the event itself.
drills.explanation: No sequence-of-tenses shift: what was future stays future under a past main verb.

drills.stem: Which subordinators introduce **time** clauses?
drills.explanation: *Kai* and *kol* fix time. *Nors* concedes; *kad* reports a statement.

drills.stem: Complete: **Nors jis dirba daug, ____ nespėja.**
drills.explanation: Concession is often answered by **vis tiek** (*all the same*).

drills.stem: **Dirbsiu, kol nebaigsiu.** What does *kol* + *ne-* signal here?
drills.explanation: A negative in the *kol*-clause often marks the **until** reading.

drills.stem: Which pairings of job are right?
drills.explanation: *Kai* answers *when* in a statement; **kada** asks the question.

drills.stem: Complete: **Kai ____, papasakosiu.** (When I return, I shall tell you.)
drills.explanation: Both clauses future: *Kai grįšiu, papasakosiu* — tense of the event, not an English present after *when*.

drills.stem: Which of these are **subordinators**?
drills.explanation: *kai*, *kol*, and *nors* subordinate. *ir* coordinates.

drills.stem: **Ateisiu, nors bus vėlu.** What does *nors* do here?
drills.explanation: *Nors* = *although*: I will come, although it will be late.

drills.stem: **Skaitau, kol važiuoju.** What is *kol* here?
drills.explanation: Two overlapping actions → *kol* = **while**.

drills.stem: Which sentences need a comma added or kept before the subordinator?
drills.explanation: *Nežinau ar…* needs the comma: *Nežinau, ar…*. The others are already correct.
